summary.text: Introduce Pell approximants by \((P_0,Q_0)=(0,1)\) and \((P_{n+1},Q_{n+1})=(P_n+Q_n,2P_n+Q_n)\), so that \(Q_n^2-2P_n^2=(-1)^n\); their approximation bounds give the exact identity \(\lfloor\sqrt2(P_n+j)\rfloor=Q_n+\lfloor\sqrt2j\rfloor\) for \(1\le j\le Q_n\), making each shifted sign block a copy of the initial block up to a parity-dependent sign. Splitting the sums according to these blocks and inducting yields \(a(P_{2k})=2k\) (and \(a(P_{2k+1})=1\)), providing arbitrarily large values.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\alpha=\sqrt2,
\qquad
 a(N)=\sum_{k=1}^N(-1)^{\lfloor k(\alpha-1)\rfloor}.
\]
We will construct infinitely many indices at which the values of this sum tend to infinity.

For an integer \(k\geq 1\), translation by the integer \(k\) gives
\[
\lfloor k(\alpha-1)\rfloor=\lfloor \alpha k-k\rfloor
 =\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor-k.                                      \tag{1}
\]
The right side is nonnegative because \(\alpha>1\). It is useful to put
\[
s(k)=\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor.
\]
Equivalently, \(s(k)\) is the integer square root of \(2k^2\): indeed,
\[
s(k)^2\leq 2k^2<(s(k)+1)^2.
\]
Thus, on defining
\[
b(k)=(-1)^{s(k)-k},
\qquad A(N)=\sum_{k=1}^N b(k),
\]
identity (1) says exactly that \(A(N)=a(N)\). We shall prove that a suitable subsequence of \(A\) is unbounded.

We use the two integer sequences \(P_n,Q_n\) defined by
\[
P_0=0,\quad Q_0=1,
\]
and
\[
P_{n+1}=P_n+Q_n,
\qquad
Q_{n+1}=2P_n+Q_n.                                      \tag{2}
\]
Their first few pairs are
\[
(P_n,Q_n)=(0,1),(1,1),(2,3),(5,7),(12,17),\ldots.
\]
These are the Pell approximants to \(\sqrt2\). Direct expansion in (2) gives
\[
Q_{n+1}^2-2P_{n+1}^2
=-(Q_n^2-2P_n^2).
\]
Since \(Q_0^2-2P_0^2=1\), induction yields the Pell identity
\[
Q_n^2-2P_n^2=(-1)^n.                                  \tag{3}
\]
We will also use a few elementary consequences of (2). For every \(n\),
\(P_n\leq Q_n\), as follows immediately by induction. For \(n\geq1\),
\(P_n>0\), and
\[
Q_n\leq \frac32P_n.                                    \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, at \(n=1\) equality \(P_1=Q_1=1\) makes this clear, and if
\(P_n\leq Q_n\), then
\[
Q_{n+1}=2P_n+Q_n\leq\frac32(P_n+Q_n)=\frac32P_{n+1}.
\]
Also \(P_n\geq5\) for \(n\geq3\), by inspecting \(P_3=5\) and observing from (2) that \(P_n\) increases thereafter. We will occasionally use the elementary numerical bounds
\[
\frac75<\alpha<\frac32,                                \tag{5}
\]
which follow by squaring positive quantities, since \(49/25<2<9/4\).

The key point is the following exact carry identity.

**Carry identity.** For every \(n\geq1\) and every integer \(j\) with
\(1\leq j\leq Q_n\),
\[
s(P_n+j)=Q_n+s(j).                                     \tag{6}
\]

We give the full proof. First consider the endpoint \(j=Q_n\). By (2),
\(P_n+Q_n=P_{n+1}\). The Pell identity determines the relevant floors.
If \(m\) is odd, then \(Q_m^2=2P_m^2-1\), and hence
\[
Q_m^2<2P_m^2<(Q_m+1)^2,
\]
so
\[
s(P_m)=Q_m.                                            \tag{7}
\]
If \(m\geq2\) is even, then \(Q_m^2=2P_m^2+1\). Since \(Q_m\geq3\),
\[
(Q_m-1)^2\leq Q_m^2-1=2P_m^2<Q_m^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
s(P_m)=Q_m-1.                                          \tag{8}
\]
Likewise, if \(m\) is odd, then
\[
2Q_m^2=4P_m^2-2,
\]
which lies between \((2P_m-1)^2\) and \((2P_m)^2\), so
\[
s(Q_m)=2P_m-1.                                         \tag{9}
\]
If \(m\geq2\) is even, then
\[
2Q_m^2=4P_m^2+2,
\]
which lies between \((2P_m)^2\) and \((2P_m+1)^2\), so
\[
s(Q_m)=2P_m.                                           \tag{10}
\]
(The required lower bounds on \(P_m,Q_m\) follow from the displayed initial values and (2).)

If \(n\) is even, then \(n+1\) is odd; using (7), (10), and (2),
\[
s(P_n+Q_n)=s(P_{n+1})=Q_{n+1}=Q_n+2P_n=Q_n+s(Q_n).
\]
If \(n\) is odd, then \(n+1\) is even; using (8), (9), and (2),
\[
s(P_n+Q_n)=s(P_{n+1})=Q_{n+1}-1
=Q_n+2P_n-1=Q_n+s(Q_n).
\]
Thus (6) holds at the endpoint.

Now suppose \(1\leq j<Q_n\), and write
\[
s=s(j)=\lfloor\alpha j\rfloor.
\]
Thus
\[
s<\alpha j<s+1.                                       \tag{11}
\]
The inequalities are strict: the right one is part of the definition of the floor, and equality on the left would make \(\sqrt2=s/j\) rational. For completeness, irrationality of \(\sqrt2\) follows by the standard parity descent. If \(2u^2=v^2\) with positive integers \(u,v\), then \(v\) is even, say \(v=2w\); the equation becomes \(u^2=2w^2\), so \(u\) is even as well. Dividing both by two gives a smaller positive solution, an impossibility by infinite descent.

To prove (6), it suffices to prove
\[
Q_n+s\leq\alpha(P_n+j)<Q_n+s+1.                        \tag{12}
\]
We separate the two signs in the Pell identity.

Suppose first that \(n\) is even. Then
\[
Q_n^2-2P_n^2=1,
\]
so, after factoring a difference of squares,
\[
\delta:=Q_n-\alpha P_n
 =\frac1{Q_n+\alpha P_n}>0.                             \tag{13}
\]
Also set
\[
R=2j^2-s^2.
\]
By (11), \(R\) is a positive integer, and
\[
\alpha j-s=\frac{R}{\alpha j+s}.                        \tag{14}
\]
The upper inequality in (12) is immediate: by (11) and \(\delta>0\),
\[
\alpha(P_n+j)-(Q_n+s)=(\alpha j-s)-\delta<1.
\]
For the lower inequality we need \(\alpha j-s\geq\delta\).

There are two cases. If \(R\geq2\), then, because \(s<\alpha j\),
\[
\frac{\alpha j+s}{2}<\alpha j\leq\alpha(Q_n-1)
  <Q_n+\alpha P_n.                                      \tag{15}
\]
The last inequality follows, for example, from (4):
\[
Q_n+\alpha P_n-\alpha(Q_n-1)
=\alpha P_n-(\alpha-1)Q_n+\alpha
\geq\left(\frac32-\frac\alpha2\right)P_n+\alpha>0.
\]
Combining (13)--(15),
\[
\alpha j-s=\frac{R}{\alpha j+s}
 \geq\frac2{\alpha j+s}
 >\frac1{Q_n+\alpha P_n}=\delta.
\]

It remains to consider \(R=1\), that is,
\[
s^2-2j^2=-1.                                           \tag{16}
\]
We claim in this exceptional case that
\[
2j\leq Q_n.                                             \tag{17}
\]
Here is the required Diophantine argument. Suppose instead that \(2j>Q_n\).
Since \(Q_n<2P_n\), this implies
\(Q_n-P_n<j\); and of course \(j<Q_n<Q_n+P_n\). Hence
\(|j-Q_n|<P_n\), or, using \(Q_n^2=2P_n^2+1\),
\[
j^2-2Q_nj+P_n^2+1<0.                                  \tag{18}
\]
A direct expansion using (16) and \(Q_n^2=2P_n^2+1\) now gives
\[
P_n^2s^2-(Q_nj-1)^2
=-(j^2-2Q_nj+P_n^2+1)>0,
\]
whereas
\[
(Q_nj+1)^2-P_n^2s^2
=j^2+2Q_nj+P_n^2+1>0.
\]
All quantities involved are nonnegative, so
\[
Q_nj-1<P_ns<Q_nj+1.
\]
Since these are integers, \(P_ns=Q_nj\). Squaring this equality and substituting
\(s^2=2j^2-1\) and \(Q_n^2=2P_n^2+1\) yields
\[
P_n^2(2j^2-1)=(2P_n^2+1)j^2,
\]
hence \(j^2=-P_n^2\), impossible. This proves (17).

Using (17), (4), and \(\alpha<2\),
\[
\alpha j+s<2\alpha j\leq\alpha Q_n<Q_n+\alpha P_n.
\]
(The last inequality follows from (4), exactly as in (15).) Therefore, from
(13), (14), and \(R=1\), we again get \(\alpha j-s>\delta\). This completes the even case of (12).

Now suppose that \(n\) is odd. If \(n=1\), then \(Q_1=1\), so there is no integer satisfying \(1\leq j<Q_1\). We may therefore assume \(n\geq3\). This time
\[
Q_n^2-2P_n^2=-1,
\]
and hence
\[
\eta:=\alpha P_n-Q_n
 =\frac1{Q_n+\alpha P_n}>0.                             \tag{19}
\]
The lower inequality in (12) follows at once from
\[
\alpha(P_n+j)-(Q_n+s)=\eta+(\alpha j-s)>0.
\]
For the upper inequality, put
\[
T=(s+1)^2-2j^2.
\]
By (11), \(T\) is a positive integer, and
\[
s+1-\alpha j=\frac{T}{s+1+\alpha j}.                  \tag{20}
\]
The desired upper bound is equivalent to
\[
\eta<s+1-\alpha j.                                     \tag{21}
\]

If \(T\geq2\), then
\[
\frac{s+1+\alpha j}{2}
\leq\alpha j+\frac12
\leq\alpha(Q_n-1)+\frac12
<Q_n+\alpha P_n.                                       \tag{22}
\]
The last inequality follows from (4), since its right side minus the preceding expression is at least
\[
\left(\frac32-\frac\alpha2\right)P_n+\alpha-\frac12>0.
\]
Equations (19), (20), and (22) imply
\[
s+1-\alpha j\geq\frac2{s+1+\alpha j}
 >\frac1{Q_n+\alpha P_n}=\eta.
\]

Finally suppose \(T=1\), so
\[
(s+1)^2-2j^2=1.                                        \tag{23}
\]
As in the even case, we need the exceptional estimate
\[
2j\leq Q_n.                                             \tag{24}
\]
If instead \(2j>Q_n\), then \(Q_n-P_n<j<Q_n+P_n\), and therefore, now using \(Q_n^2=2P_n^2-1\),
\[
j^2-2Q_nj+P_n^2-1<0.                                  \tag{25}
\]
Direct expansion from (23) gives
\[
P_n^2(s+1)^2-(Q_nj-1)^2
=j^2+2Q_nj+P_n^2-1>0
\]
and, using (25),
\[
(Q_nj+1)^2-P_n^2(s+1)^2
=-(j^2-2Q_nj+P_n^2-1)>0.
\]
Thus
\[
Q_nj-1<P_n(s+1)<Q_nj+1,
\]
so integrality forces \(P_n(s+1)=Q_nj\). Squaring and using
\((s+1)^2=2j^2+1\) and \(Q_n^2=2P_n^2-1\) once again gives
\(j^2=-P_n^2\), a contradiction. This proves (24).

By (24),
\[
s+1+\alpha j\leq2\alpha j+1\leq\alpha Q_n+1.
\]
Moreover,
\[
Q_n+\alpha P_n-(\alpha Q_n+1)
=\alpha P_n-(\alpha-1)Q_n-1
\geq\left(\frac32-\frac\alpha2\right)P_n-1>0.           \tag{26}
\]
Indeed, \(P_n\geq5\) and \(\alpha<3/2\), so the last expression is greater than
\((3/4)5-1>0\). Thus the denominator in (20) is strictly smaller than
\(Q_n+\alpha P_n\), and (19), (20), and \(T=1\) prove (21).

We have now proved (12) in every case, and hence proved the carry identity (6).

Subtracting \(P_n+j\) from the two sides of (6) gives, because all the differences are nonnegative,
\[
s(P_n+j)-(P_n+j)
=(Q_n-P_n)+(s(j)-j).                                   \tag{27}
\]
Consequently
\[
b(P_n+j)=c_n b(j),
\qquad
c_n:=(-1)^{Q_n-P_n},                                   \tag{28}
\]
for every \(1\leq j\leq Q_n\). Summing (28) for
\(1\leq j\leq m\leq Q_n\) yields the block identity
\[
\sum_{k=P_n+1}^{P_n+m}b(k)=c_n A(m).                   \tag{29}
\]
In particular, since \(P_{n+1}=P_n+Q_n\),
\[
A(P_{n+1})=A(P_n)+c_nA(Q_n).                           \tag{30}
\]
There is a second useful relation. From (2),
\[
Q_n=P_n+P_{n-1}\qquad(n\geq1),                         \tag{31}
\]
because both sides equal \(2P_{n-1}+Q_{n-1}\). Since
\(P_{n-1}\leq Q_n\), applying (29) with \(m=P_{n-1}\) gives
\[
A(Q_n)=A(P_n)+c_nA(P_{n-1}).                           \tag{32}
\]
Substitution into (30), and the fact that \(c_n^2=1\), gives
\[
A(P_{n+1})=(1+c_n)A(P_n)+A(P_{n-1}).                   \tag{33}
\]

It remains to determine \(c_n\). Subtracting the recurrences in (2) shows
\[
Q_n-P_n=P_{n-1}\qquad(n\geq1),                         \tag{34}
\]
which is also immediate from (31). Eliminating \(Q_n\) from (2) gives
\[
P_{n+2}=2P_{n+1}+P_n.
\]
Modulo \(2\), therefore, \(P_{n+2}\equiv P_n\pmod2\). Since
\(P_0=0\) and \(P_1=1\), \(P_m\) is even exactly when \(m\) is even. By (34),
\[
c_n=
\begin{cases}
 1,&n\text{ odd},\\
-1,&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}                                             \tag{35}
\]
Thus (33) becomes
\[
A(P_{n+1})=
\begin{cases}
2A(P_n)+A(P_{n-1}),&n\text{ odd},\\
A(P_{n-1}),&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}                                             \tag{36}
\]

The initial values are \(A(P_0)=A(0)=0\) and \(A(P_1)=A(1)=1\), since
\(P_1=1\) and \(s(1)=\lfloor\sqrt2\rfloor=1\). We now prove by induction on
\(k\) that
\[
A(P_{2k})=2k,
\qquad
A(P_{2k+1})=1.                                         \tag{37}
\]
For \(k=0\), these are precisely the two initial values. If (37) holds for
\(k\), first use (36) with the odd integer \(n=2k+1\):
\[
A(P_{2k+2})=2A(P_{2k+1})+A(P_{2k})=2+2k=2(k+1).
\]
Then use (36) with the even integer \(n=2k+2\):
\[
A(P_{2k+3})=A(P_{2k+1})=1.
\]
This completes the induction.

Finally, let an arbitrary integer \(M\) be given. Choose a natural number
\(k\) so large that \(2k>M\) (if \(M<0\), \(k=0\) already works; otherwise one may take \(k=M+1\)). Set
\[
N=P_{2k}.
\]
By (1) and (37),
\[
a(N)=A(N)=A(P_{2k})=2k>M.
\]
Since this can be done for every integer \(M\), the sequence \(a(n)\) is unbounded above.
